gap: No result ChatGPT got states a named lab's measured AC output for the 1 kWh candidates. Those measurements are 850–950 Wh (Notebookcheck 850 Wh for the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2; OutdoorGearLab 870 Wh for the EcoFlow DELTA 3, 890 Wh for the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2, 910 Wh for the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 and 950 Wh for the BLUETTI AC180), which works out to about 34–38 minutes on a 1,500 W heater.
standout_why: Volt & Valley, UTrendCo and Lights On Lab (all cited) say outright that their runtimes are calculated: rated Wh × an assumed 85% ÷ heater watts. They name no tester and give no measured Wh for any model. Our current page uses the same kind of calculated estimate for every row. Its only measured figure is GeekDad's run on the old Explorer 1500. Tested Watts (cited, rank 1) could not be read because WebFetch hit a certificate error and curl was not allowed, so I can't rule out that it has measurements. Its title, 'The Honest Math', suggests it calculates too.
decides: The measurements back up 'about half an hour' with lab numbers for each model instead of an assumed 85%. The candidates land within about 4 minutes of each other on high (34–38 min, or about 41 min on StorageReview's AC180 figure), so runtime doesn't decide the pick. The deciding facts stay AC headroom and weight. The AC180 tested highest in measured Wh (950 Wh at OutdoorGearLab, 1,030 Wh at StorageReview), so it gets the longest run, but it is also the heaviest. The Jackery 1000 v2 measured a respectable 910 Wh but is still rated at only 1,500 W continuous. Notebookcheck ran a 1,943 W kettle on the Elite 100 V2 without trouble, which is direct evidence that 1,800 W-class units handle a 1,500 W heater with room to spare.
